tldr: It checks out: proof checkers confirm the AI-assisted Riemann proof, a Neuralink user plays GTA 6 by thought, and Monash finds rogue ageing immune cells in mice.
window: Window: the week's best, mostly the 72 hours to 08:50 AEDT, Sun 22 Nov 2026.
notes: This week: the insula atlas and the PACER trial (19 Nov); Amazon's AI-agent report, Monash's immune map, the fly study, the sleep-and-art study and EPFL's fusion model (20 Nov).

Evidence: the Riemann proof is machine-checked by the Lean community, not yet peer reviewed; Neuralink's clip and Amazon's report are company accounts; the immune, tumour and wiring studies are in mice and the lifespan result in flies; the meal-timing link is observational; the fusion result is a model; the patch (13 people) and the bacteria computer are early tests.

post.text:
IT CHECKS OUT. ✅

The week in transhumanism:
- Lean's checkers confirm the Claude-assisted Riemann proof
- A paralysed man plays GTA 6 with a Neuralink implant
- Monash finds rogue ageing immune cells (in mice)
- A battery-free sticker shows your pulse in colour
post.alt: A 3-minute video recap of the week's best in transhumanism (22 Nov 2026): the Lean community's check of an AI-assisted Riemann proof, a Neuralink participant playing GTA 6, a test of how brain-like AI really is, faster brain-wiring maps, an atlas of the insula and pain, AI agents finding a software flaw, rogue ageing immune cells in mice, a gut enzyme and lifespan in flies, meal timing and mortality, a tumour-clearing drug pair in mice, online therapy with a peer coach, sleep loss and beauty, the FDA's second rejection of a Duchenne cell therapy, UN talks on killer robots, a battery-free pulse sticker, a fusion heating threshold and a bacteria-powered computer, with captions, sources and screenshots of the articles.

stories.title: Proof checkers confirm the Riemann proof an Anthropic mathematician wrote with Claude
stories.summary: The Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, say they have full confidence that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the 1859 Riemann hypothesis is correct, after independent checkers verified it. It's machine-checked, not yet in a journal; mathematicians still have to understand its ideas.
stories.evidence: Machine-checked proof; not yet peer reviewed

predictions.note: The Lean and Mathlib communities certified an Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted, 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis as correct; one result, not a measured speedup.

stories.title: In a Neuralink video, a paralysed trial participant plays GTA 6 with his brain implant
stories.summary: Neuralink posted a two-minute clip of an unnamed trial participant driving, flying a plane and fighting in GTA 6 by imagining small movements, such as tapping a ring finger. He used to play with a mouth stick and an iPad. No latency or accuracy figures were published, and the device is investigational, not FDA-approved.
stories.evidence: Company video of one trial participant

predictions.note: A Neuralink trial participant played GTA 6 by imagining small movements, in a company video with no published latency or accuracy figures.

stories.title: 'Brain-like' vision AI works quite differently inside, a York University test finds
stories.summary: A new 'reverse predictivity' test in Nature Machine Intelligence found AI vision models predicted recorded primate brain cells well, but the cells predicted far less of the models' insides, unlike one brain compared with another. Matching the brain's outputs doesn't mean working like it; the team released a free toolkit to check models.
stories.evidence: Peer-reviewed study of primate brain recordings

stories.title: Faster nanoscale imaging of mouse brain wiring suggests neurons nibble on their neighbours
stories.summary: Harvard Medical School and UC San Diego made electron tomography practical for brain wiring maps: about 50 times fewer images, on slices 20 times thicker, at around 15-nanometre detail. In mouse brain tissue it showed electrical synapses that maps often miss, and signs that neurons 'nibble' neighbouring cells. Whole brains are a long-term goal.
stories.evidence: Methods study in mouse brain tissue

stories.title: Electrodes in 87 people's brains map the insula, and a possible route for expectations to dial pain down
stories.summary: Using 15 years of recordings from 87 people with electrodes implanted to locate epileptic seizures, a Nature study split the insula into four zones: a pain-and-temperature body map, diffuse sensations, gut feelings with anxiety, and a front tip for attention that strongly steers the pain zones, a possible circuit for the placebo effect.

stories.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found a new hole in medical imaging software in 11 minutes
stories.summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence says a China-linked actor (moderate confidence) gave AI agents running the open-source Cairn framework one goal: 'obtain shell access'. In a September campaign against universities they found a zero-day in a medical-imaging AI app, going from mapping it to writing files in about 11 minutes; a later session got root.

stories.title: Monash maps how immune cells age in mice, including a rogue group that holds the others back
stories.summary: In mice, Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute researchers found three ways ageing disrupts the genetic instructions of CD8 T cells, the immune system's hunters of infected and cancerous cells, plus a newly identified group of ageing cells that suppresses other immune cells (Science Immunology). It could point to targets for keeping immunity strong.

stories.title: In fruit flies, an RNA-editing enzyme kept gut stem cells calm, and flies with extra lived longer
stories.summary: A Science Signaling study from China found flies lacking the enzyme ADAR in gut stem cells had runaway stem-cell growth and fast tissue ageing, while flies with extra ADAR lived longer with healthier guts. Ageing human colon samples had less of a relative, ADAR2: an association, not yet a treatment.
stories.evidence: Fruit fly study, with human and mouse tissue

stories.title: Among 31,000 Americans, a first meal after noon was linked to dying sooner
stories.summary: In 31,044 US adults aged 40+ followed for a median 8.6 years, a first meal after noon went with a 29% higher risk of death from any cause than eating first at 7-8am, and a last meal after midnight with 27% (European Journal of Clinical Nutrition). It's an association from one-day food recalls, not proof and not advice.

stories.title: In mice, a drug duo cleared breast tumours in all nine and left an immune memory of the cancer
stories.summary: Regeneron researchers paired the cancer drug Enhertu with an experimental antibody that switches on T cells through CD28 (Nature Communications). It cleared breast tumours in all nine mice, against under half on Enhertu alone, and weeks later the mice rejected the same cancer cells without more treatment. A company study in engineered mice.
stories.evidence: Mouse study by a drug company

stories.title: After chest-pain scares, online therapy with a peer coach eased anxiety more than a referral
stories.summary: In the PACER trial of 375 adults with low-risk chest pain and anxiety at six US emergency departments, self-paced online CBT with a certified peer support specialist cut anxiety scores 1.2 points more than a primary-care referral over a year, and 2.8 more in severe anxiety (JAMA Internal Medicine). A modest but real gain.

stories.title: Two short nights of sleep left students finding paintings a touch less beautiful
stories.summary: In a Baylor lab study of 68 students, two nights of about 5 hours' sleep instead of 8 lowered liking and beauty ratings of abstract paintings by about 4%, along with alertness and positive mood (Journal of Sleep Research). Small and subtle, but as Michael Scullin puts it, rest brings 'a touch more beauty'.

stories.title: The FDA turned down Capricor's Duchenne cell therapy again, saying the evidence falls short
stories.summary: The FDA sent a second Complete Response Letter for deramiocel, donor heart-derived cells for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, saying the data don't establish substantial evidence of effectiveness. Capricor says its two placebo-controlled trials met their main goals and it is reviewing its costs; Duchenne affects about 15,000 people in the US.

stories.title: UN talks on killer robots ended without binding rules; talks run to 2028
stories.summary: The UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons review conference in Geneva closed on 21 Nov with no binding rules on lethal autonomous weapons, only an agreement to keep talking through 2028. The Red Cross had urged binding rules within a year; activists said big militaries, including the US and Russia, blocked more.

predictions.note: UN talks on lethal autonomous weapons ended on 21 Nov without binding rules, only an agreement to keep talking through 2028.

stories.title: A battery-free sticker shifts colour with each heartbeat, and a phone films it
stories.summary: NTNU's OptoPatch is a thin silicone film with nanoscale grooves and octopus-style suction cups, and no electronics. Filmed by an ordinary phone, its colour shifts rebuilt a pulse waveform closely matching a clinical monitor in 13 seated volunteers. It doesn't shine light through skin, so skin tone shouldn't skew it; it still needs an app and clinical tests.

stories.title: Swiss physicists modelled a 40-year fusion puzzle: how much heating flips plasma into high gear
stories.summary: EPFL's Swiss Plasma Center built a model, in Physical Review Letters, for the heating power that switches tokamak plasma into high-confinement H-mode, first seen in 1982. It says ITER needs at least 43 MW (it's built for 73) and SPARC 26 MW (it expects 25). It was checked against existing machines; others still have to test it.
stories.evidence: A model, in Physical Review Letters

stories.title: At McGill, bacteria in a maze chip solved small maths puzzles, multiplying as they worked
stories.summary: McGill researchers built a microfluidic maze in which swimming bacteria test answers to subset-sum puzzles in parallel, solving ones of up to seven numbers. One species, Vibrio natriegens, can double every 9-12 minutes, adding 'processors' mid-calculation (Microsystems & Nanoengineering). A proof of concept; claims for bigger problems rest partly on models.

Here are the last 24 hours in transhumanism, in 3 minutes.
It checks out!
The week's biggest story: computer checkers confirm the Riemann proof Claude helped write.

Swiss physicists modelled a 40-year fusion puzzl e: how much heating flips plasma into high gear.
